in-vălĕo , ēre,
I.to be strong against, to prevail (late Lat.; “vique valebunt is the true reading,” Lucr. 2, 301 ; v. Lachm. ad h. l.; and the perf. invaluit belongs to invalesco; v. the foll. art.): “egredi conatus, invalente morbi gravitate detentus est,” Amm. 21, 15, 2 .
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
